title: Count the Money
context: Grade 3, the first working topic of the money chapter. An adult sees notes and coins being counted, which dummy money does well. What is being settled is that the number on a note or a coin is its value whatever it looks like, that notes of one kind are counted in jumps of that value, that a mixed handful is counted one kind at a time starting from the biggest, and that one price can be paid in many ways. A child who counts the pieces instead of the values will say that four notes make four rupees, and a child who finds one way to pay will think it is the only way.

writeup.why: Read the value on each note and coin, count notes or coins of one kind in jumps of their value, count a mixed handful from the biggest, and pay one price in more than one way.
writeup.look: A shop counter with a purse, the six notes and five coins as plain flat shapes, a flat tray that sorts them into tagged rows, a price tag, the Pay again and Plain list buttons, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Count the Money' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many groups of money have been counted. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A plain shop counter fills the working area. The open leather purse stands at x 100, y 214, 260 by 230. The six notes lie in a row at x 100, y 470, each a rectangle 150 by 70 in its own colour with its value in large near-black type, and the five coins lie in a row beneath them at y 560, each a disc 66 across with its value in large near-black type. Nothing else is written on a note or a coin: no portrait, no emblem, no serial number. The flat tray stands at x 400, y 214, 620 by 300. Money that lands in it is sorted into rows, one for each kind, and each row carries an amber value tag at its left, a sky blue count tag beside it and a green running total at its right. A green Total tag under the tray at x 400, y 530, 300 by 70, holds the sum of every row. The price tag hangs at x 740, y 530, 280 by 90, and holds an amount in amber. When the money in the tray is worth exactly the price, the Total turns green and a green ring runs round the tray. The Pay again button stands at x 400, y 650, 190 by 60, and the Plain list button at x 610, y 650, 190 by 60, each labelled in words. In the Plain list view the same money is a written list of rows. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing the total of the money in the tray into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag and a label. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. A note is a plain flat rectangle in its own colour and a coin a plain round disc, each with its value in large near-black type, so a value is read from the number and never from the colour. Anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because an amount is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The tray shows the last way to pay, with its rows tagged and its green total beside the price on the tag.

phases.win: a tapped note or coin lights its value in amber, and the sorted row reads from the least to the greatest
phases.does: taps a note or a coin to read its value, then sets the notes and coins in order from least to greatest
phases.goal: the number on a note or a coin is its value, and a note and a coin with the same number are worth the same
phases.says: Look at the number on each one. Which is worth the most?
phases.check: Away from the screen: two pieces of money lie on a desk, a coin with 5 on it and a note with 5 on it. Is one worth more than the other?
phases.feels: each piece lighting its value in amber as a finger touches it
phases.hands: Lay dummy notes and coins on a desk, ask each child to point to the number on each one, say its value, and put them in a row from the least value to the greatest.
phases.tries: First rung: point to the large number on the piece and say it. Second rung: put the piece next to one with a different number and say which number is bigger. Third rung: the same task with only two pieces on the counter, before the rest return.

wrong.why: a note is bigger and a coin is small, so size seems to count
wrong.move: says the paper note is worth more than the coin with the same number
wrong.screen: both pieces light the same amber value in the sorted row, and the words card says that the number on it is its value

wrong.why: every note is a different colour, and colour is the first thing a child sees
wrong.move: reads the colour of a note as its value
wrong.screen: the colours fade to half strength and only the large numbers stay, and the sorted row is made again from the numbers

phases.screen: a shop counter with the six notes and five coins in two rows beside an empty tray

phases.concept: Every note and coin has a value

phases.win: the sky blue count rises with each tap, the green total rises by one jump, and the tray settles on the full amount
phases.does: taps the pieces into the tray one at a time and counts along in jumps of the value, then types the total
phases.goal: notes or coins of one kind are counted in jumps of their value, and the total is the value counted once for each piece
phases.says: Tap them in one at a time. Count in jumps of the value.
phases.check: Away from the screen: 5 coins of Rs 2 lie in a row. Count in jumps of the value with your finger. How much is that?
phases.feels: the total stepping up by the same jump each time a piece lands

wrong.why: the two numbers are on the screen together and are easy to add by mistake
wrong.move: adds the number of pieces to the value
wrong.screen: the pieces go into the tray one at a time and the green total rises by one whole jump of the value for each, so the jumps are counted again from nought

wrong.why: counting things one by one is the habit a child already has
wrong.move: counts the pieces and says that number as the amount
wrong.screen: the sky blue count tag is lit beside the amber value tag, the two are kept apart, and the green total is shown as the value counted that many times

phases.screen: the tray with one kind of note waiting in a row beside it, a sky blue count tag and a green total tag both empty
phases.soWhat: notes or coins of one kind are counted in jumps of their value
phases.concept: Counting notes or coins of one kind

phases.win: each kind slides into its own row and the green total steps up kind by kind to the amount in the purse
phases.does: drags the kinds into the tray from the biggest value down, says the total after each kind, then types the last total
phases.goal: a mixed handful is counted one kind at a time, starting with the biggest value, and each kind is added to the total so far
phases.says: Begin with the biggest value. Add one kind at a time. What is the total now?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a purse holds 1 note of Rs 20 and 2 coins of Rs 5. Which kind do you count first, and what is the total?
phases.feels: the total growing one kind at a time from the biggest value down
phases.hands: Tip a purse of dummy money onto a desk, sort it into kinds, and count it from the biggest kind down, saying the total after each kind.
phases.tries: First rung: point to the kind with the biggest value. Second rung: say the total after that kind and after the next. Third rung: the same task with two kinds only, before the rest return.

wrong.why: the small coins are the ones nearest to hand
wrong.move: starts with the smallest coins and loses count
wrong.screen: the kinds slide into rows from the biggest value down, and the green total steps up one kind at a time so no total is lost

wrong.why: a kind lying apart on the counter is easy to forget

wrong.screen: the kinds not yet counted stay lit on the counter, and the Total tag will not take an answer until every kind has gone into the tray

phases.screen: a price tag with an amount at the right of the counter, an empty tray, and the purse full of notes and coins
phases.soWhat: one price can be paid with different notes and coins, and every way that adds up to the price pays it
phases.concept: One amount, many ways to pay

writeup.delight: On the second phase, as each piece lands in the tray the green total steps up by one jump of the value with a soft chime, and the last piece makes the whole row glow for a moment. On the fourth phase, when the money in the tray is worth exactly the price, the green ring runs once round the tray and the price tag tips its amount down onto the Total.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet counted. On the first phase the six notes and five coins lie in two rows beside an empty tray, each with its value in large type. On the second a row of one kind of note waits beside the tray, with an empty sky blue count tag and an empty green total tag. On the third a purse has been tipped out so its notes and coins lie apart on the counter, and the tray is empty with a green total at nought. On the fourth a price tag hangs at the right of the counter, the tray is empty and the purse is full. One thing moves, once: the first piece of money gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any notes and coins into the tray, with the tags, the total, the price tag and the plain list all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the value of a note or a coin, counting one kind, counting a mixed handful and paying a price, each in a small real scene.
voiceLines: A purse, a tray and a row of notes and coins, all waiting to be counted.
Look at the number on each one. Which is worth the most?
Tap them in one at a time. Count in jumps of the value.
Begin with the biggest value. Add one kind at a time. What is the total now?
Pay the price on the tag. Can you pay it a different way?
New money on the counter. Which piece will you count first?
Free play. Put any money in the tray and count it as you like.
Look at the number on each piece again. Count the jumps one at a time.
You counted every group by its values.

observations.why: the number on a note or a coin is its value, and it does not depend on what the money looks like.
observations.soWhat: a note and a coin with the same number are worth the same.
observations.observe: A Rs 10 note and a Rs 10 coin gave the same amber value tag when they were tapped, and the same step in the sorted row.

observations.why: every piece of one kind has the same value, so each piece adds the same amount.
observations.soWhat: notes or coins of one kind are counted in jumps of their value.
observations.observe: Pieces of one kind went into the tray one at a time and the green total rose by the same jump each time.

observations.why: the big values are easy to hold in mind, and each smaller kind is then added to a total already known.
observations.soWhat: a mixed handful is counted one kind at a time, biggest value first.
observations.observe: A handful counted from the biggest kind down reached the same total as one counted in any other order, but with fewer slips.

observations.why: only the value of the money matters, and different notes and coins can add to the same value.
observations.soWhat: one amount can be paid in many ways.
observations.observe: The tray rang green for two different sets of money that were worth the same as the price on the tag.

source_tool.description: A shop counter fills the working area. At the left stands a leather purse, open, and beside it the six notes and five coins of India lie in two neat rows, each a plain flat shape with its value in large near-black type and nothing else on it. A note is a rectangle in its own colour and a coin is a round disc. In the middle sits a flat tray that takes any note or coin the child taps or drags. As money lands, the tray sorts it into rows, one row for each kind. Each row carries an amber value tag, a sky blue count tag and a green running total, so the child sees the value of one, how many there are and how much they make. A green Total tag under the tray holds the sum of every row. A price tag hangs at the right of the counter and holds an amount to pay. When the money in the tray is worth exactly the price the Total turns green and the tray gets a green ring, and a Pay again button empties the tray so the same price can be paid another way. A Plain list button shows the same money as a written list. The number pad types the total. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many groups have been counted.
source_tool.art_direction: A shop counter and a purse / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Money is drawn as plain flat shapes: a note is a rectangle in its own colour and a coin a round disc, each with its value in large near-black type. There is no portrait, no emblem, no serial number and no small print on any note or coin, because a child reads the value from the number. The notes are Rs 500, Rs 200, Rs 100, Rs 50, Rs 20 and Rs 10, and the coins Rs 20, Rs 10, Rs 5, Rs 2 and Rs 1. A note is always longer than it is tall and a coin is always round.

Real everyday things hold the money and the prices: a purse, a money box, a shop shelf with a price tag on each thing, a bill on a counter, a school fair stall. The object is the thing the child counts, pays or reads, and a bare column of figures appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

An amount is always written Rs 25.50: Rs, then the rupees, then a dot, then exactly two digits of paise. Rs 5 and 5 paise is Rs 5.05, and a single digit of paise after the dot is never written. A whole number of rupees may be written without the dot, as Rs 36, or with two zeros, as Rs 36.00.

In a column sum the dots stand in one straight line, rupees to the left of it and paise to the right, with a heading Rupees over one part and Paise over the other. A carry or a borrow of one rupee is written small above the rupees column and its hundred paise above the paise column.
A price is a tag on the thing it belongs to. A bill is a table of the thing, how many, the price of one and the cost, with a rule under the last line and the total below.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a note, a coin, an amount or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a note keeps its own colour, a coin its own metal, a purse its own leather. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag, a label and a typed answer, because the dot between them is the one mark that tells a child which part is which. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Rupees, Paise, Value, How many and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the number on each piece again. Count the jumps one at a time.
voice.onNext: New money on the counter. Which piece will you count first?
voice.opening: A purse, a tray and a row of notes and coins, all waiting to be counted.
voice.onFinish: You counted every group by its values.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Put any money in the tray and count it as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Every note and coin has a value
Counting notes or coins of one kind
One amount, many ways to pay

placement.where: After each group has tipped a purse of dummy notes and coins onto a desk, counted it aloud and paid one price card in two ways, and before any total is written on the board. The tool is what keeps the value, the count and the total in three colours at once, and what turns green only when a price is paid exactly, which a purse of dummy money does not say.

answer_key.rule: The number on a note or a coin is its value. Notes or coins of one kind are counted in jumps of their value, so the total is the value counted as many times as there are pieces. A mixed handful is counted one kind at a time, starting with the biggest value, and each kind is added to the total before it. One price can be paid with different notes and coins, and every way that makes the same total pays it.
answer_key.wrong: The tray is shown again with its rows tagged, the value in amber, how many in sky blue, and the running total lit one jump at a time. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The number on a note or a coin is its value.
The note has 20 on it, so it is worth Rs 20.
The coin has 20 on it, so it is worth Rs 20.
A note and a coin with the same number are worth the same.
items.answer: Yes. Each is worth Rs 20, because the number on a note or a coin is its value.
items.question: A money box holds a note with 20 on it and a coin with 20 on it. Are the two worth the same? What is the value of each?
items.checkpoint: The number on a note or a coin is its value.
items.misconception: Thinking the paper note is worth more than the metal coin, or the other way round, because they look different.

steps: All 4 notes have the same value, Rs 50.
Count in jumps of 50: Rs 50, Rs 100, Rs 150, Rs 200.
items.question: A tray holds 4 notes of Rs 50. How much money is in the tray?
items.checkpoint: Notes of one kind are counted in jumps of their value.
items.misconception: Adding the number of notes to the value, 4 and 50, instead of counting four jumps of 50.

steps: Count the biggest first. 2 notes of Rs 100 make Rs 200.
Add the note of Rs 20. Rs 200 plus Rs 20 is Rs 220.
Add the coin of Rs 10. Rs 220 plus Rs 10 is Rs 230.
2 coins of Rs 5 make Rs 10. Rs 230 plus Rs 10 is Rs 240.
items.question: A purse holds 2 notes of Rs 100, 1 note of Rs 20, 1 coin of Rs 10 and 2 coins of Rs 5. How much money is in the purse?
items.checkpoint: Count the biggest first, then add the next kind.
items.misconception: Leaving out one kind of money, or adding the values without counting how many of each there are.

steps: Choose notes and coins whose values add up to Rs 130.
Way 1: Rs 100 plus Rs 20 is Rs 120, and Rs 120 plus Rs 10 is Rs 130.
Way 2: 2 notes of Rs 50 make Rs 100. Rs 100 plus Rs 20 is Rs 120, and Rs 120 plus Rs 10 is Rs 130.
Different notes and coins can make the same amount.
items.answer: Way 1: 1 note of Rs 100, 1 note of Rs 20 and 1 coin of Rs 10. Way 2: 2 notes of Rs 50, 1 note of Rs 20 and 1 coin of Rs 10. Both ways pay Rs 130.
items.question: A school fair stall asks for Rs 130. Show two different ways to pay it with notes and coins.
items.checkpoint: Many different sets of notes and coins can make the same amount.
items.misconception: Thinking there is only one right set of notes and coins for an amount.

A money box has 7 coins of Rs 2. How much money is in the money box?
items.final_answer: Rs 14, because 7 coins of Rs 2 make Rs 14

items.question: A purse holds 1 note of Rs 50, 1 note of Rs 10 and 3 coins of Rs 2. How much money is in the purse?
items.final_answer: Rs 66, because Rs 50 plus Rs 10 is Rs 60 and Rs 60 plus Rs 6 is Rs 66

items.question: A kite costs Rs 85. Name one way to pay for it with notes and coins.
items.final_answer: One way is 1 note of Rs 50, 1 note of Rs 20, 1 coin of Rs 10 and 1 coin of Rs 5. Another way is 4 notes of Rs 20 and 1 coin of Rs 5

items.question: One tray holds 3 notes of Rs 200. Another tray holds 7 notes of Rs 100. Which tray has more money, and how much more?
items.final_answer: The tray with 7 notes of Rs 100. 7 notes of Rs 100 make Rs 700 and 3 notes of Rs 200 make Rs 600. Rs 700 minus Rs 600 is Rs 100, so it holds Rs 100 more

items.question: Which two of these pay exactly Rs 36? A: 1 note of Rs 20, 1 coin of Rs 10 and 3 coins of Rs 2. B: 1 note of Rs 20, 1 coin of Rs 10 and 3 coins of Rs 1. C: 3 coins of Rs 10 and 3 coins of Rs 2.
items.final_answer: A and C. A is Rs 20 plus Rs 10, which is Rs 30, and Rs 30 plus Rs 6 is Rs 36. C is Rs 30 plus Rs 6, which is Rs 36. B pays only Rs 33

items.question: A money box holds 1 note of Rs 500, 3 notes of Rs 50, 4 coins of Rs 10 and 5 coins of Rs 2. How much money is in the money box?
items.final_answer: Rs 700, because Rs 500 plus Rs 150 is Rs 650, Rs 650 plus Rs 40 is Rs 690 and Rs 690 plus Rs 10 is Rs 700

items.question: A toy costs Rs 175. Pay for it with exactly 3 notes and 1 coin. Which notes and which coin do you use?
items.final_answer: 1 note of Rs 100, 1 note of Rs 50, 1 note of Rs 20 and 1 coin of Rs 5, because Rs 100 plus Rs 50 is Rs 150, Rs 150 plus Rs 20 is Rs 170 and Rs 170 plus Rs 5 is Rs 175

teaching_notes: Give each group a purse of dummy notes and coins before the tool opens, and ask them to tip it out, count it aloud and say the total. Always ask what the number on a note or a coin is called before any count starts, and wait for a child to say value rather than saying it for them. When a group has notes of one kind, have them count in jumps of the value with a finger on each note. For a mixed handful, ask which kind to count first and wait for the biggest. Once one way to pay a price is found, ask for another and ask whether it gives the same amount. Go back to the question at the start of the chapter once a handful can be counted. Use fresh amounts: the printed groups are the child's to match and pay.
generation_prompt: Build a money-counting tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A shop counter fills the working area. At the left stands an open leather purse and beside it the six notes and five coins of India lie in two rows as plain flat shapes: a note is a rectangle in its own colour and a coin is a round disc, each with only its value in large near-black type and no portrait, emblem or serial number. In the middle a flat tray takes any note or coin the child taps or drags and sorts it into rows, one for each kind, each row with an amber value tag, a sky blue count tag and a green running total. A green Total tag under the tray holds the sum of every row. A price tag at the right holds an amount to pay, and the tray gets a green ring when the money in it is worth exactly the price. A Pay again button empties the tray, and a Plain list button shows the money as a written list. The number pad types the total. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of groups counted. Every amount is written Rs 25 or Rs 25.50 in plain letters and the rupee sign is never drawn. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
